false_positives.candidate:
Building SQLite ID lists performs quadratic string allocation

For SQLite batches over 999, each iteration formats the complete accumulated values string again. The final SQL text for a 32,767-ID batch is hundreds of kilobytes, but this loop repeatedly copies all prior content and can allocate several gigabytes cumulatively. The new 40K-row test exercises this path, and orphan-tag cleanup can hit it as well. Build the list with strings.Builder or a byte slice/strconv.AppendInt so each ID is appended once.

Non-SQLite deletes can exceed database bind-parameter limits

The non-SQLite path creates one bound parameter for every fetched ID and does not cap or chunk the list. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable; values above 65,535 will fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL prepared statements (and lower limits apply to some supported dialects), causing every cleanup run to fail. The old delete subquery did not bind an ID per row. Split ids into dialect-safe chunks, or validate and enforce a conservative maximum batch size.

The renamed second-run test no longer performs a second cleanup run

This subtest now creates a fresh set of nine annotations, already exactly three per annotation type, and invokes the cleaner only once. Its zero-affected assertion only proves that an already compliant dataset is untouched; it no longer verifies the stated behavior of rerunning max-count cleanup after a preceding run has removed excess annotations. Run the cleaner twice within this subtest and assert that only the second invocation affects zero rows.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled on response completion

The timeout context is derived from the request context captured by the handler. For normal HTTP/API-server requests that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, while this work is deliberately still running asynchronously. Consequently Legacy.Create can be canceled before or during its write even though the caller has already received a successful unified-storage response; the same issue exists in the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines at lines 110, 135, and 163. Use a writer-owned background context (while preserving required values) with its own timeout and shutdown lifecycle rather than the request cancellation context.

Independent async mirror writes do not preserve write ordering

Every successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or sequencing. For example, a unified delete followed by a create of the same name can run in the opposite order in legacy storage: the create completes first and the delayed delete then removes the newly created object. Consecutive updates can similarly leave an older version as the final legacy state. This makes the legacy copy diverge permanently; queue or serialize mirror operations by resource, or apply a monotonic version/sequence check.

Legacy update re-evaluates the original update callback instead of mirroring the unified result

Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified store's old object before this goroutine starts, but Legacy.Update is given the original objInfo and will evaluate UpdatedObject again against a potentially stale or different legacy object. UpdatedObjectInfo is explicitly old-object dependent and can perform transformations or have side effects, so the two stores can receive different payloads. The prior implementation materialized the update and wrapped the unified result for the legacy write; retain an immutable materialized result for the asynchronous mirror operation.

A unified NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup

This early return covers NotFound errors, so a resource that exists only in legacy storage is left there when it is deleted through mode 3. The previous implementation explicitly continued to Legacy.Delete for a unified NotFound while returning the unified error to the caller. Leaving the stale legacy object visible through legacy APIs also risks resurrecting it if the migration is rolled back; preserve the NotFound cleanup path, asynchronously if needed.

Legacy replication has no concurrency or queue bound

A goroutine is spawned for every successful write, and each can remain active for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). A slow or unavailable legacy backend therefore lets normal unified writes accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and backend connections with no backpressure, risking process resource exhaustion under write load. Use a bounded worker pool/queue and define behavior when it is full.

Mode 3 unit tests do not verify that the asynchronous legacy write occurs

Both storage wrappers share the same mock.Mock, their expectations have identical method signatures, and the tests never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. Thus the synchronous unified call can satisfy the configured method pattern and a regression that never invokes Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection would still pass. Use distinct backend mocks plus a channel/eventual assertion to verify exactly one legacy call after successful unified writes and no legacy call after primary failures.

The mode 3 integration test assumes an asynchronous legacy mirror is immediately visible

The newly added mode 3 subtests execute doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s writes and then immediately requires the legacy playlist list to contain those objects at this assertion (with similar immediate legacy reads later). Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so scheduler or CI load can make these assertions fail nondeterministically. Poll for eventual legacy consistency with a bounded timeout, or otherwise synchronize the test with the mirror operation.

false_positives.candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests

Load the entire `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]` chain in the translation/loading path, or otherwise make fallback loading global rather than controller-specific.

false_positives.candidate:
The host allowlist is bypassed after an HTTP redirect

`TopicRetriever` checks only the hostname of the initial URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects and this method does not validate the redirect destination. An attacker who can use an open redirect on the configured embeddable host can make the Discourse server request arbitrary HTTP endpoints, including internal services or cloud metadata addresses; the fetched response may then be imported into a public topic. Disable redirects or validate every redirect target, including resolved IP addresses, against the allowed destination policy.

The outer transaction lets post-processing jobs run before the imported post commits

`PostCreator#create` deliberately enqueues post-processing work after its own `Post.transaction`, but that nested transaction joins this surrounding `Topic.transaction`. Consequently `PostCreator` enqueues jobs while this outer transaction is still open, so a separate Sidekiq connection can run before it can see the post. If `TopicEmbed.create!` subsequently fails (for example, due to the unique URL index during a concurrent import), the outer transaction rolls the post back after jobs and MessageBus events have already been emitted for it. Defer those side effects with an after-commit hook or restructure the creation so the post and embed commit before jobs are enqueued.

This method calls `open` with an HTTP URL but does not require `open-uri`, which is what extends `Kernel#open` to handle URLs. The only new `require 'open-uri'` is in the unrelated `PollFeed` job. With feed polling disabled (the default), `retrieve_topic` reaches this method without loading `PollFeed`, so normal `Kernel#open` treats the URL as a local filename and raises instead of retrieving the article. The throttle lease is established with `SETNX` and its expiry is applied in a separate Redis command. If the process dies or the Redis connection fails after `setnx` succeeds but before `expire` succeeds, the key has no TTL. Every later non-staff retrieval for that URL sees the key and returns without importing it, leaving the embed on its loading page indefinitely. Set the value and expiration atomically (for example, Redis `SET ... NX EX 60` or a Lua script).

The conversion only handles `href`/`src` values beginning with `/`. Ordinary relative references such as `images/photo.jpg`, `../next-page`, and fragment links remain relative to the Discourse topic/embed URL rather than the imported article, so common images and links break. Protocol-relative URLs are also incorrectly rewritten as paths on the source host. Resolve URLs with the article URL as the base (for example via `URI.join`) instead of concatenating only root-relative paths.

The command no longer declares `--category`/`-c`, and the replacement `TopicEmbed.import_remote` call has no way to pass a category. Existing import automation using that documented Thor option now fails with an unknown switch, while invocations without it can no longer import threads into the requested category and instead use the default. Multipart uploads have no server-side input limit before ImageMagick processing

The new 10 MB limit is only enforced by the browser and for URL downloads; a client can POST a multipart file directly with any size. An upload-capable user can therefore submit very large or decompression-bomb images and consume substantial worker CPU, memory, disk, and temporary-file space. Enforce a raw byte and image-pixel limit on the server before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

For normal multipart uploads, `tempfile.path` is Rack's generated temporary filename rather than the original `.gif` filename. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated GIF path only when `from` ends in `.GIF`; this call therefore takes the regular ImageMagick path, whose input is `#{from}[0]` and contains only the first frame. false_positives.candidate:
The selected destination calendar is not passed to calendar providers

Although `createEvent` accepts `externalId` and `EventManager` supplies each destination's ID, this call invokes the provider with only the complete `CalendarEvent` array and the credential ID. Office 365, Lark, and CalDAV currently select `destinationCalendar[0]`, so when iterating a second collective host they attempt to create the event in the first host's calendar (often with an unauthorized credential). The `externalId` is only copied into the resulting reference later and does not affect where the event is created. Pass the selected destination through to the provider, or have every provider select the entry matching the credential/target.

Collective host calendars are discarded when the first host has no destination calendar

The initial event value is `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. The collective-host calendars are then added with `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)`, which silently does nothing for that case. A collective booking where another host has a calendar but the organizer does not therefore has no destination calendars and no host calendar event is created. Initialize this field as an empty array or assign a new array when adding host calendars.

Only the first collective destination is persisted on the booking

The booking write connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`, so all secondary host destination calendars are lost once the request completes. Deferred scheduling paths such as confirmation and payment webhooks rebuild their `CalendarEvent` from the singular `booking.destinationCalendar` and consequently create an event only for the main host. Persist all destination-calendar selections (or reliably reconstruct them from the collective hosts) before supporting deferred collective bookings.

Video booking references lose their credential ID

`referencesToCreate` now sets `credentialId` to `undefined` for every non-calendar result. Dedicated video results previously retained `result.credentialId`; removing it creates video BookingReferences without the credential needed to update or delete the meeting. For example, the cancellation handler only deletes a video meeting when its reference has a credential ID, leaving these meetings orphaned. Preserve `result.credentialId` for video results.

Location updates create calendar references without calendar or credential identifiers

`updateLocation` now copies `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId` into new references, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` does not populate either field in its returned EventResult. Every calendar reference appended by the location-update flow will therefore have no external calendar ID or credential ID. Later updates/cancellations cannot target the original event and may fall back to all connected calendars. Return the input credential/calendar identifiers from `updateEvent`, or derive them from the source reference before writing the new one.

Recurring collective cancellation deletes only one calendar reference per occurrence

For each recurring occurrence this code uses `.find(...)` to select the first calendar reference, then invokes deletion through every calendar credential. With multiple collective-host references, the remaining references are never selected with their own credential and calendar ID; the outer reference loop merely repeats the same first-reference work. Secondary host events remain on their calendars after cancelling all remaining occurrences. Iterate every occurrence reference and resolve/use that reference's credential ID.

Reschedule cleanup collapses multiple host credentials of the same integration

The cleanup map is keyed only by integration type, so multiple collective references such as two `google_calendar` host calendars are all deleted using whichever credential was last inserted for that type. A host credential normally cannot delete another host's calendar event; Google treats a 404 as a successful delete here, so the failure can be silent and leave the old event behind. Resolve the credential by each BookingReference's `credentialId` rather than by its type.

The public booking webhook payload changes destinationCalendar shape without compatibility handling

CalendarEvent is serialized into booking webhook payloads, as demonstrated by the webhook E2E test. Changing `destinationCalendar` from an object/null to an array changes the JSON contract for every existing webhook consumer that reads fields such as `destinationCalendar.externalId` or expects null. The PR provides no payload versioning, compatibility field, or migration documentation, so consumers will break when hosts have a destination calendar.

No automated test covers the multi-destination collective lifecycle

The PR adds creation, update, and cancellation paths for multiple destination calendars but does not test a collective booking with distinct host credentials/calendars. A test should verify that each provider receives its own selected calendar and that the resulting references allow reschedule and cancellation to update/delete every host event. The existing webhook expectation change only checks an empty-array payload and would not detect the first-destination and missing-reference regressions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Request-reschedule returns before integration deletions finish

The async callback supplied to `forEach` is discarded. Since the calendar branch now awaits `getCalendar`, neither the calendar import nor `deleteEvent` is awaited by the mutation, and there is no rejection handler for either operation. The booking is already marked cancelled and the mutation can complete while its calendar/video event remains active; a failed dynamic import or provider deletion is an unhandled rejection. Await a collected `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` for these callbacks before completing the reschedule operation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the lack of error handling for the awaited calendar import (`getCalendar`). The candidate issue specifically notes that 'there is no rejection handler for either operation... a failed dynamic import or provider deletion is an unhandled rejection' and suggests using `Promise.allSettled` (along with fixing the unawaited `forEach`), which covers the golden comment's concern about handling import failures gracefully.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Calendar and video deletion promises are discarded during rescheduling

`Array.prototype.forEach` does not await an async callback. The new `await getCalendar(...)` makes each calendar deletion asynchronous before `deleteEvent` is even invoked, but the surrounding `try/catch` exits immediately and the reschedule flow sends the email/returns without waiting for or observing any deletion failure. Rejections from either the import or provider call bypass this catch, and the old external event can remain active after the booking has been marked cancelled. Await a `Promise.all`/`Promise.allSettled` over `bookingRefsFiltered.map(...)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: using `forEach` with an `async` callback for calendar/video event deletions, which causes promises to not be awaited, bypassing surrounding `try/catch` blocks, and recommends using `Promise.all` with `map()`.

false_positives.candidate:
The dynamic imports are all started eagerly rather than on demand

Each `import("./...")` expression is executed while the `appStore` object is initialized. Consequently, merely importing `@calcom/app-store` starts loading and evaluating every integration module, including integrations unrelated to the request. This defeats on-demand loading and keeps cold-start CPU, memory, and chunk-loading costs coupled to the full app catalog. Store loader functions instead (for example, `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke only the selected loader at the call site.

Recurring cancellation does not wait for calendar deletions

The async callback passed to `forEach` is never joined. In this branch it now first awaits `getCalendar`, so the parent handler can reach its later `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` before the callbacks have populated `apiDeletes`; those callbacks push the deletion result only after the deletion has already completed. The handler can therefore remove booking references and return success while recurring external calendar events are still being deleted, and provider/import failures become unhandled. Build and await a promise per credential/booking deletion instead of using `forEach`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deleting a client leaves its V2 authorization resource and policies behind

The client-removal listener now runs only when the legacy `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` feature is enabled. In a V2-only deployment, a `ClientRemovedEvent` is ignored, while the per-client resource and its scope permissions live under the admin-permissions resource server and have no foreign-key relationship to the deleted target client. They remain orphaned indefinitely; if a client with the same internal ID is later restored/imported, `getOrCreateResource` resolves the old resource by name and the deleted client's grants become effective for the new client. Add V2-specific resource/policy cleanup on client removal.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the removal listener is gated only on the V1 ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ flag, so with V2 alone enabled the cleanup never runs and permissions are left orphaned. The candidate talks only about client removal rather than role/client/group removal, but the underlying problem is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients are not upgraded with the Clients schema

`init` returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. A realm that enabled FGAP V2 before this change therefore keeps only the old Users resource/scopes: it never receives the Clients all-resource or the new `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, and `map-roles-composite` scopes. Creating a per-client permission then attempts to attach every Clients scope and fails with `No scopes found`, while global-client permission evaluation can also encounter a missing resource. Add a non-destructive schema backfill/migration path for existing admin-permissions clients.

The all-clients manage permission does not grant list/view access

`canView()` recognizes only the all-clients `view` scope, unlike `canView(ClientModel)`, which reaches `canManage(client)` through `canConfigure(client)`. The inherited `canList()` and client-scope listing checks depend on this zero-argument method, so an administrator granted only the all-clients `manage` scope can create, update, and delete clients but cannot list them. This contradicts the intended manage permission behavior and makes the added `testManageAllClients` listing expectation fail. Include `manage` here (or delegate through `canManage()`).

Role-mapping checks drop the built-in manage-clients authorization

`canMapRoles`, `canMapCompositeRoles`, and `canMapClientScopeRoles` only evaluate V2 authorization resources. They do not preserve the `MANAGE_CLIENTS` admin-role fallback used by the other client checks, so a normal realm-management administrator with `manage-clients` is denied client-role assignment and composite-role changes whenever FGAP V2 is enabled unless separate V2 policies are created. The map-role checks need to honor the built-in management role (and the intended manage-scope inheritance, if applicable) before evaluating the resource scope.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. A global group view grant is treated as permission to manage groups

`canManage()` evaluates both `view` and `manage` on the all-groups resource. Consequently, a principal granted only the `view` scope passes `requireManage()` for operations that do not yet have a concrete group, including `POST /groups`. That permits creating top-level groups and moving an existing group to the top level, despite the policy granting read-only access. Only the `manage` scope should satisfy this method.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say canManage() accepts the VIEW scope as well as MANAGE, so view-only users get manage access. Both say only MANAGE should satisfy it. The candidate adds concrete consequences, but it is the same bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-member discovery uses authorization resource IDs as realm group IDs

The callback receives an authorization `Resource`, but passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission()` and adds that same value to the returned set. Authorization resource IDs are generated independently from the realm group ID; the domain group ID is the resource name established by `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup()`. This makes the name lookup in `hasPermission()` miss the individual resource and sends opaque authorization IDs as `UserModel.GROUPS` to the user provider. Scoped group-member grants therefore do not filter users correctly, and an all-groups member grant can filter every user out. Use the resource name/domain group ID for both operations.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. groupResource.getId() is passed to hasPermission and added to the granted set, while the actual group ID is the resource name. This mismatch breaks the name lookup and puts the wrong IDs into UserModel.GROUPS filtering.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions realms are never initialized with the new Groups schema

`init()` returns as soon as an admin-permissions client already exists. Realms created with the previous V2 schema therefore retain no `Groups` resource, no group scopes, and no group-specific resources after an upgrade. Creating a group scope permission then fails because `getScope()` cannot find the new scope, while group evaluators cannot resolve the all-groups resource. Initialization needs to reconcile missing schema scopes/resources for an existing admin-permissions client, or an explicit migration is required.

Resources created for individual groups are not assigned the Groups type

When `getOrCreateResource()` creates a resource for a group ID, it updates its scopes but never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)`. `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` discovers scoped group grants using `findByType(..., "Groups", ...)`, so these individual resources are not discovered at all. As a result, group-member grants are omitted from the group filter used by user search/count operations; authorized users can disappear from paged searches and counts. Newly created resources need their schema resource type assigned.

Listing groups re-evaluates a global authorization policy for every group

The previous `canViewGlobal` short circuit was removed, so every group in a non-hierarchical listing now calls `groupsEvaluator.canView(group)`. Under V2, even an all-groups `view` grant causes each call to look up/evaluate the authorization resource and its policies before falling back to the all-groups resource. This changes a global-view list from one policy evaluation to one evaluation per returned group (and the same regression exists in `GroupResource.getSubGroups`), which is expensive for realms with many groups. Cache `groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and only evaluate individual groups when it is false.

true_positives.reasoning: Both say getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of BouncyCastle, so they describe the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`CryptoProvider` is a public ServiceLoader SPI, and adding `order()` as an abstract method makes every provider compiled against the previous interface incompatible. During `CryptoIntegration.init`, the comparator invokes `order()` on such a provider and throws `AbstractMethodError`, preventing startup even when that provider was the only valid provider before this change. Make this a default method with a legacy-safe priority (or otherwise provide a compatibility adapter) so existing implementations remain loadable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments raise the same problem: adding an abstract order() method to the CryptoProvider SPI breaks existing implementations. The candidate elaborates on how the failure shows up, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-priority crypto providers are silently selected by classpath order

The new selection logic accepts multiple providers with the same highest priority and chooses whichever ServiceLoader returns first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` are all assigned priority 200, so a classpath containing both default and FIPS providers no longer fails fast as it did previously; it can select the non-FIPS default provider based on classpath/resource ordering. This can silently disable the intended FIPS crypto integration. Reject ties for the highest priority (while still allowing lower-priority providers such as the authz client provider), or make selection explicitly configured and deterministic.

ECDSA raw signature conversion accepts and ignores trailing signature bytes

`concatenatedRSToASN1DER` copies exactly `signLength` bytes but never verifies that `signature.length` equals `signLength`. Any bytes after the expected R||S value are silently discarded, so distinct raw JOSE ECDSA signature values with the same prefix are converted to the same DER value and can be accepted by a verifier. Short inputs also fail with an unchecked array-copy exception rather than being treated as invalid signatures. Validate the exact fixed signature length up front and throw the declared `IOException` for malformed input.

The redirect traversal limit now splits deep traces that previously merged

`SpansBuffer` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans`, but the previous enforcement in `_load_segment_data` was removed and the Lua script always retains exactly 1,000 members. Callers configured with a lower cap can now retain up to 1,000 spans, while callers configured with a higher cap are silently limited to 1,000; even the default behavior changes from accepting 1,001 spans to retaining 1,000. Weighted counts are truncated to an integer

Client sample rates are floats and are not restricted here to rates whose inverse is integral; for example, a 0.3 sample rate produces a non-integral weight. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled on response completion

The timeout context is derived from the request context captured by the handler. For normal HTTP/API-server requests that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, while this work is deliberately still running asynchronously. Consequently Legacy.Create can be canceled before or during its write even though the caller has already received a successful unified-storage response; the same issue exists in the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines at lines 110, 135, and 163. Use a writer-owned background context (while preserving required values) with its own timeout and shutdown lifecycle rather than the request cancellation context.

Independent async mirror writes do not preserve write ordering

Every successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or sequencing. For example, a unified delete followed by a create of the same name can run in the opposite order in legacy storage: the create completes first and the delayed delete then removes the newly created object. Consecutive updates can similarly leave an older version as the final legacy state. This makes the legacy copy diverge permanently; queue or serialize mirror operations by resource, or apply a monotonic version/sequence check.

Legacy update re-evaluates the original update callback instead of mirroring the unified result

Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified store's old object before this goroutine starts, but Legacy.Update is given the original objInfo and will evaluate UpdatedObject again against a potentially stale or different legacy object. UpdatedObjectInfo is explicitly old-object dependent and can perform transformations or have side effects, so the two stores can receive different payloads. The prior implementation materialized the update and wrapped the unified result for the legacy write; retain an immutable materialized result for the asynchronous mirror operation.

A unified NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup

This early return covers NotFound errors, so a resource that exists only in legacy storage is left there when it is deleted through mode 3. The previous implementation explicitly continued to Legacy.Delete for a unified NotFound while returning the unified error to the caller. Leaving the stale legacy object visible through legacy APIs also risks resurrecting it if the migration is rolled back; preserve the NotFound cleanup path, asynchronously if needed.

Legacy replication has no concurrency or queue bound

A goroutine is spawned for every successful write, and each can remain active for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). A slow or unavailable legacy backend therefore lets normal unified writes accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and backend connections with no backpressure, risking process resource exhaustion under write load. Use a bounded worker pool/queue and define behavior when it is full.

Mode 3 unit tests do not verify that the asynchronous legacy write occurs

Both storage wrappers share the same mock.Mock, their expectations have identical method signatures, and the tests never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. Thus the synchronous unified call can satisfy the configured method pattern and a regression that never invokes Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection would still pass. Use distinct backend mocks plus a channel/eventual assertion to verify exactly one legacy call after successful unified writes and no legacy call after primary failures.

The mode 3 integration test assumes an asynchronous legacy mirror is immediately visible

The newly added mode 3 subtests execute doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s writes and then immediately requires the legacy playlist list to contain those objects at this assertion (with similar immediate legacy reads later). Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so scheduler or CI load can make these assertions fail nondeterministically. Poll for eventual legacy consistency with a bounded timeout, or otherwise synchronize the test with the mirror operation.

postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The new downsize definition replaces, rather than overloads, the existing API

Ruby does not overload methods by argument count. This definition replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts = {})` definition, so existing callers using the prior width/height API now either raise `ArgumentError` for five arguments or treat `max_height` as `opts` for four arguments and fail when `optimize` indexes it as a hash. Preserve both call forms in a single method or use a differently named helper.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out the same problem: the second downsize definition overrides the first, which took separate max_width and max_height arguments, so existing callers break. Ruby has no overloading, so the earlier method becomes unreachable.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side attachment limits no longer honor site configuration

`validateUploadedFile` is used for both `image` and `attachment`, but this change replaces the type-specific `max_<type>_size_kb` setting with a fixed 10 MB limit for both. Non-image attachments are not downsized by the controller, so sites with a smaller attachment limit now let users upload files that the server rejects, while sites allowing attachments over 10 MB are incorrectly blocked in the browser. Keep the larger raw-file allowance limited to images being downsized and continue using `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the hardcoded 10MB limit replaces the per-type max_<type>_size_kb site setting, so client and server limits diverge. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Multipart uploads have no server-side input limit before ImageMagick processing

The new 10 MB limit is only enforced by the browser and for URL downloads; a client can POST a multipart file directly with any size. Any oversized image is passed through up to five ImageMagick conversions before `Upload.create_for` gets a chance to enforce the configured stored-file limit. An upload-capable user can therefore submit very large or decompression-bomb images and consume substantial worker CPU, memory, disk, and temporary-file space. Enforce a raw byte and image-pixel limit on the server before invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

Oversized animated GIF uploads lose their animation despite the setting

For normal multipart uploads, `tempfile.path` is Rack's generated temporary filename rather than the original `.gif` filename. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated GIF path only when `from` ends in `.GIF`; this call therefore takes the regular ImageMagick path, whose input is `#{from}[0]` and contains only the first frame. Consequently, an oversized animated GIF is converted to a static image even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. Preserve/pass the original format when selecting the conversion path and write through a suitably typed temporary file.

The retry limit does not ensure the image meets the configured size limit

The loop stops after five 80%-dimension resizes without checking that the resulting byte size is below `max_image_size_kb`. File size is not reduced by a fixed ratio when dimensions are reduced, especially for PNGs and already-compressed images, and valid installations can configure a limit low enough that five passes are insufficient. The subsequent upload will then be rejected by the existing size validation (or stored over the intended limit), so users still cannot upload the large image the feature is meant to handle. Continue until the byte target is met or no further useful reduction is possible, and return a clear failure when it cannot be met.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
The top-level route does not resolve the added template

`topicUnsubscribe` is registered as a top-level route, so Ember will look up its default template under the route name (for example `topic-unsubscribe`), not `topic/unsubscribe`. The added template is registered as `topic/unsubscribe`, which is the name for a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route. Since this route does not set `templateName` or render that template explicitly, navigating from the email link will not render the unsubscribe page and its notification-state control. Rename the template to match the top-level route or explicitly set `templateName: 'topic/unsubscribe'`.

A GET request changes a user's notification preference without CSRF protection

The new `unsubscribe` action is reached through a GET route and mutates `TopicUser` state. GET requests are not protected by Rails' normal CSRF checks, and this action is also exempted from the XHR check. A third-party page can cause a logged-in user's browser to request `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` and silently lower that user's notification level; mail-client/link-preview prefetching can have the same effect. Render a confirmation on GET and perform the mutation via a CSRF-protected POST/PUT (or otherwise use a recipient-bound, deliberate confirmation flow).

Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser's notification-change bookkeeping

Saving the `TopicUser` record directly only changes `notification_level`; it does not set `notifications_changed_at`, mark `notifications_reason_id` as `user_changed`, invoke the observer path, or publish the MessageBus notification that other sessions use to refresh their state. In particular, a row whose reason remains `NULL` can later be auto-promoted from muted to tracking by `TopicUser.update_last_read`, because that method treats a NULL reason as eligible for auto-tracking. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so an explicit unsubscribe remains explicit and connected clients are notified.

The shared unsubscribe translation now requires an option MessageBuilder does not default

`unsubscribe_link` now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`, but `Email::MessageBuilder` only supplies a default `user_preferences_url`; `unsubscribe_url` is optional and is only added on the notification-mail path in this change. Any existing caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without the new option will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` while building the text or HTML body, preventing delivery. Preserve the existing builder contract by defaulting `unsubscribe_url`, or use a separate translation/conditional paragraph when no per-topic URL is available.

false_negatives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The webhook helper cannot reliably update .env on GNU/Linux

`sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed, the separate empty argument is treated as an input file, causing sed to exit with an error; because the script does not use `set -e`, it can still print that GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was updated. This makes the added test helper unreliable on Linux. Use a portable temporary-file replacement or select the appropriate `sed -i` form per platform and fail when the replacement fails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: `sed -i ''` is macOS/BSD syntax and fails on GNU/Linux. The candidate adds extra detail about the missing `set -e`, but the core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not refresh the displayed cache status

The delete-cache mutation only invokes the optional onSuccess callback. The connectedCalendars query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt is not invalidated, and this wrapper explicitly disables refetch-on-window-focus. When the wrapper is used without an onChanged callback (which its props permit), a successful deletion leaves the old timestamp and delete action visible until a full remount or reload. Invalidate viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on successful/settled cache deletion, as the disconnect mutation already does.

Migration fabricates the last-updated time for every existing cache entry

Adding this non-null column with DEFAULT NOW() stamps every pre-existing CalendarCache row with the migration time. The new UI presents this value as "Last updated", so immediately after deployment old cache data will be reported as having been refreshed at deployment even though its value may be nearly expired. Backfill from an existing source such as expiresAt minus the cache TTL where valid, or represent legacy timestamps as unknown until the cache is refreshed.

Each cache warm rewrites all selected-calendar rows for the credential

After populating cache data for the supplied selectedCalendars, this credential-wide update touches every SelectedCalendar row with that credential, including calendars and event types that were not part of the refresh. Because SelectedCalendar has an updatedAt field, this is a bulk physical update solely to change timestamps; the new cache-status endpoint reads CalendarCache.updatedAt instead, so this write does not affect the displayed status. Cache refreshes can be triggered repeatedly by webhook/cache workflows, causing avoidable row locks, WAL/MVCC churn, and contention for credentials with many event types. Remove this touch or limit it to the rows actually refreshed if another consumer truly needs it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fixed-host working-hours validation rejects split schedules and permits slots past closing time

`end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` rather than `slotEndTime`, so a slot that starts before the end of a host's hours but finishes after it is treated as valid. Also, using `workingHours.find` with an "outside this interval" predicate makes every slot invalid for a host with multiple windows on the same day: a 10:00 slot in a 09:00-12:00 window is rejected when the 13:00-17:00 window is inspected, and vice versa. Since this check is the new fixed-host guard after round-robin availability has been aggregated, it can both hide valid slots and allow bookings that overrun a fixed host's availability. The check should test the actual slot end and accept when any applicable working-hours range fully contains the slot.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says `end` is calculated from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, which is the golden issue. It also raises a second point about split schedules, but that does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fixed-host override validation does not require a booking to fit inside an override window

The callback marks a slot unavailable only when it is wholly before an override or starts strictly after it; any slot overlapping either edge falls through `dateOverrideExist` and is accepted. For example, a 30-minute slot from 10:45 to 11:15 is accepted for a 10:00 to 11:00 override. The `.find` also stops on the first nonmatching range, so with 09:00-10:00 and 14:00-15:00 overrides, a valid 14:00 slot is rejected because it is after the first range. Additionally, the empty-override branch at line 114 compares two distinct Dayjs objects with `===`, so a 10:00-10:00 blackout is not detected and can admit a slot beginning at 10:00. This can book a round-robin event while its fixed host is unavailable; the code needs to require the full slot interval to be contained in at least one override range.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that the empty-override branch compares two distinct Dayjs objects with ===, so the check fails. That is the same bug the golden comment describes, even though the candidate also raises other issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override end times use the start-time timezone offset across DST transitions

`offset` is derived only from `override.start` and is reused when converting `override.end`. An override can span a daylight-saving transition, where the endpoint has a different organizer or invitee UTC offset. For example, a New York override from 01:00 to 03:00 on the spring-forward date spans 06:00 to 07:00 UTC, but applying the start's UTC-05 offset to the 03:00 endpoint converts it to 08:00 UTC and exposes an extra unavailable hour. Resolve the organizer/invitee offset separately for each endpoint (using the override's local date/time) before calculating its local minutes.

The primary fixed-host round-robin behavior has no automated regression test

The new test exercises a personal event with one user. The existing round-robin test uses `hosts: []`, which means its round-robin users are all classified as non-fixed and never execute the new `fixedHosts.every(...)` path. There is therefore no test for the reported scenario of a round-robin event with both a fixed host and a loose host, where a loose host creates a candidate slot outside the fixed host's date override. Add that scenario and assert that slots outside the fixed host's override are absent.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count updates lose failures when cron invocations overlap

The retry count is calculated from the value read by `findMany` and then written back. If two authorized cron invocations select the same unscheduled reminder, both can observe (for example) `retryCount = 0`, both attempt scheduling, and both write `1`; the row is then retried again despite already having failed twice. The same overlap can cause multiple scheduling attempts for one reminder. Claim the reminder/attempt atomically with a conditional update or lock, and increment in the database rather than writing a stale value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. The retry count is computed from a stale read, so concurrent runs can lose increments. Both recommend incrementing atomically in the database.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes reminders for every delivery method

The `retryCount > 1` branch is not constrained to `WorkflowMethods.SMS`. This endpoint will therefore delete any `WorkflowReminder` with more than one retry, including a future email or WhatsApp reminder, even though the retry behavior being implemented is for SMS scheduling. Keep `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` in the retry-exhaustion branch (and ensure it only targets the intended unscheduled state) so shared reminder records cannot be removed by this SMS cron.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch is missing the SMS method filter, so it deletes Email and WhatsApp reminders too.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no usable destination are never counted as failed

Failure accounting is entirely inside the `if (message?.length && sendTo)` block. When an SMS reminder has an empty or missing recipient number (or no generated message), the loop silently skips it without setting `scheduled` or incrementing `retryCount`, so the cron continues selecting it until its scheduled date. This leaves a class of invalid SMS reminders with the exact indefinite rescheduling behavior the retry limit is intended to stop; treat an unusable destination/message as a terminal or retryable failure and update/delete the reminder accordingly.

The public `findMany` API was removed without a compatibility path

`InsightsBookingService` previously exposed `findMany(findManyArgs)`, which executed an authorized Prisma query while preserving caller-supplied selection, ordering, pagination, and `where` options. It has been removed and replaced only with `getBaseConditions()`, which is not an equivalent API and does not execute a query or accept those options. Existing consumers of this service will fail TypeScript compilation on `.findMany`, and a consumer migrated only to this fragment can easily lose its previous query constraints. Keep a compatible `findMany` implementation (using the raw-condition approach internally if necessary), or migrate every production call site and preserve each caller's query semantics in this change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The sync token schema strips expiry and provider token fields

The computed keys are literal `"[object Object]"` property names, not catch-all/index signatures; the second one also overwrites the first. Zod objects strip unknown fields by default, so in sync mode parsing a normal response returns only `access_token`, then line 26 adds a synthetic `refresh_token`. Expiry values, real refresh tokens, scopes, and provider-specific fields are discarded before callers persist them, producing unusable credentials (for example Zoom computes an invalid expiry and Google loses its stored refresh token).
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problematic code: the computed keys [z.string().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema. The golden comment says this throws a runtime error. The candidate says the keys become literal "[object Object]" names and that unknown fields get stripped. The consequences described differ, but the flagged bug is the same invalid computed-key schema.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google refresh persists the Zod safe-parse wrapper as the credential key

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), unlike the previous `googleCredentialSchema.parse` call which returned the credential object itself. This update stores that wrapper in `Credential.key`; on the next request `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` receives no top-level token fields and rejects the saved Google credential, breaking the integration after its first refresh.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a safeParse wrapper, and that wrapper is persisted as the credential key instead of the parsed data.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync mode changes refresh results into an incompatible response type

The sync branch always returns the native Fetch `Response`, while several supplied refresh functions return an SDK response or a token object and their callers continue to consume those shapes. Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` directly, and the Zoho integrations read Axios `tokenInfo.data`; none of these callers parses the Fetch response body. Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore causes undefined-token errors or writes invalid credentials for these integrations.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: in sync mode, refreshFunction returns a fetch Response while callers like Google (res.data) and HubSpot (token object) expect integration-specific shapes, which causes runtime errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync mode changes refresh results into an incompatible response type

The sync branch always returns the native Fetch `Response`, while several supplied refresh functions return an SDK response or a token object and their callers continue to consume those shapes. Google reads `res.data`, HubSpot reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` directly, and the Zoho integrations read Axios `tokenInfo.data`; none of these callers parses the Fetch response body. Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore causes undefined-token errors or writes invalid credentials for these integrations.

The sync endpoint path returns a fetch Response, while callers expect an SDK or Axios shape and read res.data, so the token is undefined and errors follow. The candidate explicitly names the Google res.data case, which matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin sends a credential ID as the Cal.com user ID

`refreshOAuthTokens` constructs its request with `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId`, which is the Credential primary key rather than the owning user's ID. Credential and user IDs are unrelated, so the remote source will generally fail to find the user and can return credentials for another user whose ID happens to match the credential ID.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens is passed credentialId where userId (calcomUserId) is expected, which causes incorrect user lookups during credential sync.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce creates its client with the stale access token after refreshing

The new code obtains and persists `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, but the subsequent `jsforce.Connection` is initialized with `credentialKey.access_token`, the pre-refresh token. If that old token is expired—the condition that necessitates a refresh—the immediately returned client authenticates with the expired token rather than the token just received.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: after the token refresh, jsforce.Connection is still initialized with the stale credentialKey.access_token instead of the refreshed one. The candidate does not mention instance_url, but the core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
`prisma` is used without being imported

The new credential update references `prisma`, but this module has no `@calcom/prisma` import. Type-checking fails with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, preventing the app-store package from building.

Credential-sync refresh requests contain no authentication

The configured credential-sync endpoint receives only a predictable user ID and app slug. The helper does not send `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` under `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, nor any other authentication or signature, so an endpoint implemented according to this client cannot verify that a request came from its Cal.com instance. If that endpoint returns access tokens based on these fields, unauthenticated callers can request users' credentials.

Credential sync cannot identify which credential to replace

The payload identifies only a user and app, while the database permits multiple credentials for the same user and app (for example, the Google OAuth callback creates a credential on every connection). `findFirst` has no ordering and updates an arbitrary matching credential, leaving other stale credentials in place. Syncing one external account can therefore overwrite a different account's tokens and make bookings use the wrong calendar.

Salesforce bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint

Unlike the other modified integrations, Salesforce performs its refresh directly against Salesforce and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`. Consequently, when credential sharing is enabled, the configured source-of-truth endpoint is never queried for Salesforce and the implementation still depends on the locally stored refresh token.

Zoom sends a route name instead of its app slug to the sync endpoint

This sends `zoomvideo` as `appSlug`, but the Zoom integration's installed app ID/slug is `zoom` (as used by `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`). A source endpoint that keys credentials by the Cal.com app slug will not find Zoom credentials for this request, so Zoom token refresh fails only when syncing is enabled.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Direct booking reschedules bypass the new durable cancellation flow

The normal booking reschedule flow calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)`, which performs an immediate SendGrid cancellation and returns without setting `WorkflowReminder.cancelled`. This reintroduces the exact capped-pending-cancellation failure the PR is intended to avoid: when SendGrid rejects the immediate cancellation, the helper catches the error, the reminder stays `cancelled = null`, and the cron query will never retry it. Rescheduled bookings through this endpoint can therefore still send their old reminders; use the persisted `cancelled` path (or mark it for cron retry when the immediate call fails).
true_positives.reasoning: Both point at the immediateDelete=true path of deleteScheduledEmailReminder, where SendGrid is cancelled immediately but the WorkflowReminder DB record is not updated or deleted, unlike the false path which marks it cancelled. The candidate frames the consequence as a missed cron retry rather than an orphaned record, and it does not mention the omitted DELETE call. The core flaw, a missing DB update and inconsistency with the cancelled path, is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
The SendGrid client used for cancellation is never authenticated

This route only calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, but the new cancellation request at line 57 is made through the separate `@sendgrid/client` instance. `@sendgrid/mail` does not configure that client's authorization header, so the cancellation POST will be rejected by SendGrid and the error is only logged. Configure `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` in this route before calling `client.request`; otherwise cancelled reminders remain scheduled and are sent.

A cancellation shortly before a reminder is due is not processed before the email sends

Cancellation is now deferred exclusively to a cron job that runs every 15 minutes. If a booking is cancelled after a cron invocation and its scheduled reminder is due before the next invocation (for example, a reminder due in five minutes), no SendGrid cancellation is attempted before `sendAt`, so the reminder is still delivered. The one-hour query horizon does not solve this because it is only evaluated when cron next runs. Near-term reminders need an immediate/guaranteed cancellation path or a worker cadence that completes before their send time.

One failed cancellation prevents all later reminders in the batch from being cancelled

The entire loop is enclosed by one `try` block. If `client.request` fails for any reminder, execution exits the loop immediately and skips cancellation of every remaining reminder; it also skips the accumulated database deletes for prior successful requests. A permanently invalid or transiently failing batch can consequently leave other valid, imminent cancelled reminders untouched until a later run, and can repeatedly block them. Handle failures per reminder and persist successful cancellations independently so one bad SendGrid request cannot block the rest.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklisted guest emails can be bypassed with casing changes

BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS is normalized to lowercase, but each submitted guest address is compared without lowercasing. `updateLocation` now copies `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId` into new references, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` does not populate either field in its returned EventResult. With multiple collective-host references, the remaining references are never selected with their own credential and calendar ID; the outer reference loop merely repeats the same first-reference work. Changing `destinationCalendar` from an object/null to an array changes the JSON contract for every existing webhook consumer that reads fields such as `destinationCalendar.externalId` or expects null. When a worker is deemed hung, the code starts a replacement for the same shard group without killing the old worker; the old process is then no longer tracked and can continue flushing/producing concurrently. Repeated health failures leak workers and can duplicate segment output. Legacy replication has no concurrency or queue bound

A goroutine is spawned for every successful write, and each can remain active for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). A slow or unavailable legacy backend therefore lets normal unified writes accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and backend connections with no backpressure, risking process resource exhaustion under write load. Use a bounded worker pool/queue and define behavior when it is full.

Duration metrics are attributed to the wrong storage backend

A Storage.Create failure is recorded through recordLegacyDuration even though no legacy call was made; the same mistake occurs for Storage.Update at line 129. Conversely, the async Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 is recorded with recordStorageDuration after storage was already recorded at line 159. This produces false backend latency/error rates and can hide primary-storage failures during the migration rollout.

Mode 3 unit tests do not verify that the asynchronous legacy write occurs

Both storage wrappers share the same mock.Mock, their expectations have identical method signatures, and the tests never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. Thus the synchronous unified call can satisfy the configured method pattern and a regression that never invokes Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection would still pass. Use distinct backend mocks plus a channel/eventual assertion to verify exactly one legacy call after successful unified writes and no legacy call after primary failures.

The mode 3 integration test assumes an asynchronous legacy mirror is immediately visible

The newly added mode 3 subtests execute doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s writes and then immediately requires the legacy playlist list to contain those objects at this assertion (with similar immediate legacy reads later). Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so scheduler or CI load can make these assertions fail nondeterministically. Poll for eventual legacy consistency with a bounded timeout, or otherwise synchronize the test with the mirror operation.
